opening.headline: Processing all requests through the same path results in wasted costs and limits; therefore, we explore a method of dividing request processing tiers based on the waiting time each request can tolerate.
body: Customer responses waiting in chat windows, analyses that only need to be completed by tomorrow morning, and thousands of summaries generated all at once at month-end—all these tasks have vastly different waiting times. However, when these requests are processed through a single standard pathway, non-urgent work consumes expensive real-time pathways and quotas, causing user-waiting requests to be starved by large-scale operations.

In this class, we compare the characteristics of three processing tiers—Priority, Flex, and Batch—based on documentation from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic within the same framework. Then, we establish criteria to classify requests by delay tolerance and assign them to respective tiers, and examine cases where requests are categorized at the boundaries.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: First, it can describe the characteristics of flexibility and batch processing.
Requests can be classified into appropriate handling levels based on the allowable delay.

screens.title: All requests are using the same path and same price.
screens.lead: First, take a look at a service that handles all requests through a single path. It's best to read the comparison between the current structure on the left and the separated structure on the right in the diagram.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the current structure, where three types of requests enter through a single pipe, with the separated structure divided into three separate paths.
labels: Waiting time: several seconds / several hours / within one day

paragraphs: One company operates three AI tasks. The customer service chatbot waits for users to respond on screen. A nightly log analysis task only needs to produce results by morning. The end-of-month report generation task must generate thousands of documents and complete within a single day.

Currently, all three tasks follow the same standard path. This leads to two problems: non-time-sensitive work consumes the cost and limits of the real-time path, while conversely, user requests waiting for responses get delayed by large-scale tasks. This creates a structure where both cost and user experience suffer.

The fundamental issue is that requests take different amounts of time to respond, yet there is no standard to distinguish between these response times. Providers offer all low-cost tiers instead of setting different tiers with varying speeds and latency tolerances, thereby leveraging this variability.

callout.label: Questions to be answered in this class
callout.text: Based on the latency tolerance, to which service level should each request be sent?

screens.outro: First, let's consider the requests present in your services.

screens.title: Consider the allowable delay per request
screens.lead: First, judge for yourself among the three example requests, then select one. Afterward, the instructor's summary will be presented. No answers are submitted or entered.

items.prompt: How long can the customer wait for a response in the chat window?
items.answer: Since the user is waiting in front of the screen, a response must be delivered within a few seconds. Such requests are critical in terms of latency and stability, and in many cases, it is worthwhile to incur additional costs to meet these requirements.

items.prompt: How about an analysis that concludes by morning meeting time tomorrow?
items.answer: Since the results are needed several hours later, it is acceptable for a single request to take a few minutes. Instead of accepting delays, you may choose to reduce the value.

items.prompt: What about thousands of summaries generated all at once at month-end?
items.answer: It can be completed within a day, and there's no need to immediately see responses for each individual request. The approach of handling requests in batches and retrieving the results later is appropriate.

items.prompt: Have we ever categorized each request of our service based on such criteria?
items.answer: If you have never categorized before, it's likely that all requests are going through the same path. Next, we'll examine sequentially what options are available and what the classification criteria are.

screens.outro: Now let's confirm what each of the three processing levels obtains and what it sacrifices.

screens.title: Three processing tiers: Priority, Flex, Batch
screens.lead: Compare the service levels based on the comparison items in the Gemini API documentation. Pay attention to how price, latency, and reliability are balanced against each other.

data.caption: Gemini API Processing Tier Comparison
rows: Best effort; if capacity is insufficient, it is deferred.
Target completion time: 24 hours, most cases finish much sooner
Asynchronous calls bundled as a request
data.notes: Priority is a tier that charges a premium price to ensure low latency and high stability. Flex is a pull-based approach where each request immediately receives a response, but when capacity is insufficient, it is treated with lower priority. Batch is an asynchronous approach where requests are grouped and results are retrieved later. Therefore, although Flex and Batch both offer the same 50% discount, their different invocation mechanisms make them incompatible with each other. If no priority is specified for a request, it is handled by default. As shown in the table, price and latency move in opposite directions: to receive responses quickly, you must pay more, and to reduce cost, you must wait longer.

screens.outro: Let's see how this structure is named and constrained in OpenAI and Anthropic.

screens.title: Three Company's Response Capabilities and Limitations
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify how the provider-specific rapid tier, slow low-cost tier, placement, and constraints are configured.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body:
**Fast Tier.** Priority is designated with `service_tier` as `priority` and is processed before standard and Flex traffic.

**Slow Low-cost Tier.** Flex reduces costs by 50% compared to standard, but introduces variable latency and availability at best-effort levels. Users may receive a 503 Service Unavailable error if the system reaches capacity limits.

**Batch.** The Batch API costs 50% of the standard rate, has a target completion time of 24 hours, and typically completes much faster. Input is prepared as a JSON Lines file.

**Constraints.** If no tier is specified, the request is processed as standard.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
**Fast tier.** Fast mode provides up to 2.5x faster speeds than standard for services directly interacting with users. `service_tier` can be used with `fast` or `priority`.

**Slow low-cost tier.** Flex offers lower costs at the expense of slower response times and potential temporary resource unavailability. It is well-suited for model evaluation, data augmentation, and asynchronous tasks. Long-running tasks should increase their timeout duration.

**Batch.** The Batch API collects requests into a JSONL file and processes them, reducing costs by 50% and utilizing a separate, larger rate limit pool, completing within 24 hours.

**Constraints.** Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex usage.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body:
**Fast Tier.** Fast mode increases output token speed by up to 2.5x when specifying `speed` as `fast`, at the cost of a premium price. The improvement is in output speed, not the time to generate the first token.

**Slow Low-Price Tier.** This document bundle does not include a separate description for the low-cost tier corresponding to Flex.

**Batching.** The Message Batches API can hold up to 100,000 requests or 256MB per batch and typically completes within one hour, reducing costs by 50%. It expires if not completed within 24 hours.

**Rate Limits.** Fast mode has its own dedicated rate limit; exceeding it results in a 429 error.

screens.outro: Now that we know the shape of the grade, let's express the criteria for assigning requests to grades as a policy.

screens.title: Delay Tolerance Classification Table and Grade Assignment
screens.lead: The following is an example policy that summarizes grade assignment by request type. The field names are hypothetical configurations for illustrative purposes, and the grade values follow those specified in the document. Review the judgment order alongside the right-side explanations.

data.code:
#Processing grade assignment table by request type (example)
routes:
  - request: "Customer consultation response"
    wait: "Second second, the user is waiting in front of the screen"
    tier: standard
    fast_option: "Queries where response speed is critical receive priority or fast review."
  - request: "Employee document summary"
    wait: "Allow variations in delay at the frame level"
    tier: flex
    fallback: "Retry with standard on failure"
  - request: "Nightly analysis report"
    wait: "a few hours"
    tier: flex
    retry: "Retry design to address transient failures"
  - request: "Monthly report, large-scale assessment"
    wait: "Within one day"
    tier: batch
    mode: "Asynchronous, result retrieval logic required"

notes.note: Requests that users are waiting for follow standard defaults. Only a subset of queries, where speed is critical, are evaluated for Priority or Fast settings. Applying such settings to all requests would significantly increase costs due to the premium pricing.

While waiting is acceptable for a few minutes, Flex prioritizes availability and thus provides a standard fallback path. If this path is unavailable, users will encounter an error when capacity is insufficient.
The work requiring results only until morning must be designed with temporary failures possible, and thus retry mechanisms should be implemented instead of simply lowering values.

This is a bulk operation where you do not need to immediately see the response for each request. Completion time is assumed to be up to 24 hours, with sufficient buffer time built into the schedule. Since it is asynchronous, logic is required to retrieve the results. Input is prepared as a file containing one request per line.

screens.outro: The decision is organized in the order of three questions: Is the user waiting in front of the screen? If not, when is the result needed? And, can the operation be retried even if it fails or experiences delays in the interim? Now, let's apply these criteria to a specific case.

screens.lead: The instructor assigns a rating to each of the three tasks in the initial case. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Verify three tasks
steps.body: Examples include a customer service chatbot, nightly log analysis, and monthly report generation. All three tasks use the same model but differ in wait time. This difference serves as the starting point for tier assignment.

steps.title: Chatbots are based on standards.
steps.body: Since users are waiting in front of the screen, variable-delay Flex or one-day scheduling is not appropriate. Use standard paths by default, and only evaluate queries with priority or fast response times where response speed is critical.

steps.title: Nightly analysis uses Flex.
steps.body: Since the result is only needed by morning, you can tolerate delays and reduce the cost. Flex offers a 50% discount compared to standard rates. However, if the capacity is insufficient, requests may be delayed or fail, so retry mechanisms should be designed.

steps.title: The end-of-month report is sent by batch.
steps.body: We bundle thousands of requests into batches. Assuming a target completion time of within 24 hours, we schedule with some buffer time. Some providers also use separate rate limit pools, which reduces impact on real-time traffic.

steps.title: Break down usage by grade level
steps.body: Even with the same model, costs and limits vary by service tier. You must break down usage reports by service tier to verify cost savings.

steps.title: Schedules are retained as documents.
steps.body: Document the classification results in a table to ensure the team applies the same criteria. When new requests arise, assign ratings by adding a new row to the table. Include fields such as request type, allowable delay, assigned rating, and response action upon failure in the table, so future justifications can be reviewed without re-evaluating the basis.

screens.outro: Next, I'll discuss two ambiguous requests placed at the boundary.

screens.title: Explanation: How are requests at the boundary divided?
screens.lead: Compare how the instructor makes decisions by alternately selecting between two requests. The key to the judgment is whether the user is waiting or when the result is used.

states.label: Request A: Summary allowing delays and retries at the second level
states.body: Summary document allowing employees to request handling with a delay of up to a few minutes and retrying. Users can wait for a few minutes without issue. This request follows a path that first attempts Flex, and falls back to standard behavior if capacity is insufficient or limits are reached. Flex operates on a pull-based motivation model, which makes it suitable for requests where users need to wait. Conversely, using Priority would incur excessive costs for such requests. Batch processing is asynchronous and thus does not align with requests where users are waiting.

states.label: Request B: Full data reevaluation once per day
states.body: This is a batch job that re-evaluates all data once per day. Even after receiving the results, they are not immediately usable, and there's no need to view responses for individual requests right away. This use case fits well with batch processing. It costs 50% less, and providers that use separate rate limit pools do not have to compete with real-time traffic or rate limits. Instead, batch processing is asynchronous, requiring logic to retrieve results, and introduces additional operational complexity compared to simple calls. Both approaches represent a cost-reduction choice in scenarios where users do not require immediate results. The underlying principle is the same: the higher the acceptable delay, the lower the cost grade; the lower the acceptable delay, the greater the cost incurred for speed and stability.

screens.outro: I will proceed to summarize the principles of judgment drawn by comparing the two requests.

screens.title: Summary: The delay tolerance determines the processing tier.
screens.lead: Summarize the content discussed so far into a single criterion. Please read the following paragraphs in sequence.

paragraphs: Processing tiers are choices that trade off speed, cost, and availability. Priority and Fast impose premium pricing for speed and stability. Flex maintains synchronous calls but sacrifices latency and availability to reduce cost. Batch processing takes on large volumes asynchronously at reduced cost.

The criterion for determining priority is the waiting time for a request. By considering whether the user is waiting, when the result is needed, and whether retries are possible in the case of delay or failure, a priority is assigned to each request. The classification results should be documented in a priority matrix to ensure the team applies the same standards.

When mixing tiers, you should also verify their relationship with other purchasing models. For example, OpenAI Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex plans. When tiers are split, costs and limits are divided accordingly, so usage is also segregated and monitored by tier.

glossary.def: This is a premium processing tier prioritizing latency and stability. In Gemini, the service_tier is designated with priority, while in OpenAI, it can be used in Fast mode.
Instead of reducing the value, it is a deferred call grade with variable latency and availability at best-effort level.
This approach bundles large requests and handles them asynchronously, retrieving the results later. All three providers reduce costs by 50%.
A method of determining an appropriate processing level based on the waiting time per request.

misconceptions.myth: Flex and layout are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: Flex is a request-driven, synchronous model where each request returns an immediate response, while batching is an asynchronous model that handles requests in groups and retrieves results later. Because the invocation patterns differ, they cannot be interchanged.

misconceptions.myth: A higher grade is always better.
misconceptions.fact: Priority and Fast incur premium charges. They should be used only for time-sensitive requests; applying them to all requests results in a significant cost increase.

misconceptions.myth: The batch is too slow to use.
misconceptions.fact: According to Anthropic's documentation, most runs complete within one hour, and Gemini also completes most tasks significantly faster than the target time. However, a 24-hour upper limit should be set to allow for some buffer in scheduling.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Latency tolerance determines the processing tier.
Priority and Fast are for speed, while Flex and layout are for cost reduction.
Flex and layout offer lower cost instead of compromising on delay and availability.
When mixing levels, you also verify the applicable scope of other purchase methods such as reservation processing capacity.
